University students often need income, experience and enough time to study. The best jobs for university students balance all three.

For most students, the strongest options are tutoring, on-campus work, research assistance, library work, retail, hospitality, administration, freelancing and selected online jobs. The right choice depends on your timetable, existing skills, location and career plans.

A private tutor may earn more per hour, while a campus assistant may offer a shorter commute. A retail job can be easier to secure, whereas a research assistant role may offer stronger long-term CV value.

How We Ranked These Student Jobs

A high hourly rate does not automatically make a job suitable for students. I considered five practical factors:

  • Flexibility around lectures
  • Compatibility with assignments and exams
  • Ease of finding work
  • Earning potential
  • CV and career value

Think about it this way. If a job pays £2 more per hour but requires a long commute and unpredictable shifts, it may provide less real value than a nearby role with a slightly lower rate.

1. Private Tutor

Private tutoring is one of the best jobs for university students who have strong knowledge in a particular subject.

You could teach mathematics, science, English, languages, music, economics or basic programming. Sessions may take place online, at the learner’s home or in a public study space.

For example, a civil engineering student could tutor GCSE mathematics for two hours on Tuesday evening and one hour on Saturday morning. That schedule provides income without filling every weekday.

Best for: Students with strong academic results

Advantages: Flexible hours, good earning potential and useful communication experience

Challenges: Lesson preparation and cancelled sessions

Tutoring can also strengthen applications for teaching, education, consulting and customer-facing careers.

2. On-Campus Assistant

On-campus work is often a practical choice because you can travel directly from a lecture to your shift.

Universities may employ students in reception, student services, computer rooms, sports facilities, event teams and departmental offices. Duties can include answering routine questions, preparing rooms, checking bookings or updating records.

Check your university careers service and student union before searching general job websites. Some campus vacancies are advertised internally first.

For example, the IUB Library’s student employment programme shows how universities can provide paid practical experience within a campus environment.

Best for: First-year students and students with busy timetables

Advantages: Short commute and academic-friendly scheduling

Challenges: Limited vacancies

3. Research Assistant

Research assistant work is valuable for students considering postgraduate study or research-based careers.

You may collect data, organise references, transcribe interviews, prepare spreadsheets, conduct literature searches or support laboratory work. Duties depend on your department and the project.

Ask lecturers, supervisors and department administrators about opportunities. Some roles are never listed on large job boards.

Best for: Students interested in research or postgraduate study

Advantages: Strong academic reference and analytical experience

Challenges: Competitive applications and limited availability

The pay may not always exceed retail or hospitality work. Its value often appears later when an employer asks for evidence of structured research or problem-solving.

4. Library or Departmental Assistant

Library jobs suit students who prefer predictable responsibilities and a quieter environment.

Typical duties include shelving books, helping at a service desk, processing returns, preparing study areas and supporting library events. Departmental assistants may organise files, answer emails or update records.

Best for: Students who want lower-stress part-time work

Advantages: Calm setting and regular duties

Challenges: Fewer vacancies and limited hours

5. Student Ambassador

Student ambassadors represent their university at open days, applicant events, school visits and online information sessions.

You may give campus tours, answer questions, welcome visitors or explain your experience as a student. The role suits people interested in communication, marketing, education or recruitment.

You do not need to be the most confident person in the room. Clear explanations and a helpful attitude matter more than performing.

Best for: Confident communicators

Advantages: Networking, public speaking and university experience

Challenges: Work may be seasonal

6. Admin Assistant

An admin assistant role can give you useful office experience before graduation.

Your duties might include managing calendars, replying to emails, updating spreadsheets, preparing documents, taking notes or organising files. These tasks develop accuracy, time management and professional communication.

A student who supports an office for eight hours a week can gain experience with Microsoft Excel, Google Workspace, CRM systems and document management.

Best for: Business, law, humanities and social science students

Advantages: Transferable office skills

Challenges: Some roles require fixed hours

7. Retail Assistant

Retail is one of the easier routes into paid student work. Shops often need evening, weekend and seasonal staff.

You may serve customers, operate tills, replenish stock, process deliveries or help with online orders. Retail can be tiring during busy periods, but it develops communication, teamwork and problem-solving skills.

Best for: Students wanting regular weekend or evening shifts

Advantages: Frequent vacancies and straightforward entry requirements

Challenges: Long periods standing and busy seasonal work

Before accepting an offer, ask whether the employer provides guaranteed hours and how far ahead the rota is issued.

8. Hospitality Worker

Restaurants, cafés, hotels and event venues regularly recruit students.

Roles include waiting staff, kitchen assistant, front-of-house worker, event staff and hotel receptionist. Hospitality can provide quick employment, although shifts may finish late and workloads may change suddenly.

Best for: Students who need work quickly

Advantages: Many entry-level vacancies

Challenges: Late finishes, busy shifts and variable rotas

9. Barista

Barista work can suit students who have free mornings, afternoons or weekends.

The job includes preparing drinks, serving customers, handling payments, cleaning equipment and following food-safety procedures. Many cafés provide training.

Ask whether the rota can change during exams. A café may advertise flexible work but still expect regular availability.

10. Freelance Writer or Designer

Freelancing is flexible, but it works best when you already have a useful skill.

Possible services include:

  • Blog writing
  • Proofreading
  • Graphic design
  • Video editing
  • Presentation design
  • Translation
  • Illustration
  • Website content

Build a small portfolio before applying for larger projects. Three strong examples are usually more useful than a long list of unsupported claims.

Best for: Creative and digital students

Advantages: Remote work and portfolio development

Challenges: Irregular income and client management

Never pay a recruiter to access ordinary freelance work. Avoid clients who request your password, one-time code or excessive unpaid work.

11. Social Media Assistant

Small businesses, charities, societies and student organisations often need support with social media.

You may schedule posts, write captions, create short videos, answer routine comments or prepare simple performance reports. This can provide useful experience for marketing, communications and media careers.

A simple portfolio containing six sample posts and one content calendar can help you stand out.

Best for: Marketing, media and communications students

Advantages: Flexible work and commercially useful experience

Challenges: Some clients expect constant availability

Agree your working hours and response times before starting.

12. Data-Entry or Operations Assistant

Data-entry work may involve updating records, checking information, transferring details between systems or preparing basic reports.

Some positions are remote or hybrid. However, data-entry adverts also attract scams because they often promise unusually high pay for very simple tasks.

A genuine employer should explain the company, duties, payment terms and selection process. You should not need to pay a registration fee.

Best for: Students with basic computer skills

Advantages: Clear duties and flexible working arrangements

Challenges: Low pay in many entry-level roles

13. Care or Support Worker

Care work may suit students studying nursing, psychology, social work, health or education.

Duties can include supporting daily activities, accompanying clients, preparing meals or helping with community activities. Training, background checks and specific eligibility requirements may apply.

Confirm the employer’s training, supervision, insurance and shift expectations before accepting the role.

Best for: Students seeking health or social-care experience

Advantages: Meaningful and relevant work

Challenges: Physically and emotionally demanding

14. Delivery Rider

Delivery work offers considerable control over your hours.

You may work during busy evening periods, weekends or quieter academic weeks. However, calculate your real income after fuel, maintenance, insurance, mobile data and equipment.

A shift that appears profitable may provide much less after those costs.

Best for: Students needing maximum flexibility

Advantages: Quick entry and adjustable shifts

Challenges: Weather, traffic and operating expenses

15. Peer Mentor or Writing-Centre Assistant

Peer mentors support other students with study habits, academic writing, orientation or subject-specific learning.

You may hold one-to-one meetings, assist with workshops or help students find university services. This experience can support future applications in teaching, counselling, education and student support.

Best for: Academically strong students with good communication skills

Advantages: Credible campus experience

Challenges: Limited places

Best Jobs for Students with No Experience

If you have never had a formal job, start with positions that value reliability and availability:

  • Retail assistant
  • Barista
  • Hospitality worker
  • On-campus assistant
  • Delivery rider
  • Data-entry assistant
  • Event staff
  • Warehouse assistant

Your coursework, volunteering, society activities and group projects can still demonstrate useful skills.

Best Online Jobs for University Students

Online jobs for university students include:

  • Online tutoring
  • Freelance writing
  • Graphic design
  • Video editing
  • Social media assistance
  • Virtual administration
  • Proofreading
  • Data-entry work

Remote work is not automatically easier. It requires self-discipline, reliable internet access and clear communication with clients.

Students specifically searching for work-from-home opportunities should compare payment terms, workload and employer credibility before accepting a role.

Best Jobs for Building Your CV

Choose work that creates evidence you can explain later:

  • Research assistant
  • Student ambassador
  • Admin assistant
  • Peer mentor
  • Social media assistant
  • Course-related internship
  • Customer-service role

Write down what you achieved. “Worked in a shop” is weaker than “Served customers, processed payments and resolved routine complaints during busy weekend shifts.”

How Many Hours Should a Student Work?

There is no universal answer. Your course intensity, commute, health and financial situation all matter.

Many students begin with 8 to 12 hours per week and adjust after understanding their workload. Reduce your hours during examinations if possible.

Pay and Minimum Wage

Pay depends on age, location, employer, experience and contract type.

In the UK, from April 2026, the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is £12.71 per hour. The rate for workers aged 18 to 20 is £10.85, while the 16 to 17 and apprentice rates are £8.00. Check the latest National Minimum Wage rates before assessing an offer.

Also check:

  • Whether training is paid
  • Whether tips are shared
  • Whether travel time is paid
  • Whether the role is employed or self-employed
  • When payment will be made
  • Whether minimum-wage rules apply

How to Find a Student Job

Start with your university careers service, student union and department noticeboards. A university careers service can connect students with internships, employers and application support. ULAB, for example, describes its careers centre as supporting students with employment and career guidance.

You can also search:

  • University job portals
  • Local employers near campus
  • Reputable job boards
  • Company career pages
  • Student societies
  • Professional networks
  • Personal referrals

Use specific searches such as “part-time library assistant near Manchester” or “online mathematics tutor for GCSE students” rather than searching only for “student jobs”.

How to Apply Without Experience

Your CV should show evidence, even if you have not held a formal job.

Include:

  • Relevant modules
  • Coursework projects
  • Volunteering
  • Society responsibilities
  • Technical skills
  • Languages
  • Availability
  • Academic or professional references

For example, replace “good communication skills” with:

Presented a five-person research project to 30 classmates and answered questions from the audience.

That statement gives the employer something concrete to remember.

Student Job Scams to Avoid

Be cautious when an advert:

  • Promises unusually high pay for very little work
  • Requests an upfront payment
  • Uses only a messaging app
  • Asks for your banking password or one-time code
  • Pressures you to recruit friends
  • Sends you a cheque and asks for money back
  • Refuses to provide a written job description

Search for the employer independently and verify the email domain. Never share passwords, PINs or account access. Students have been warned about fake job adverts, payment fraud and impersonation scams by official organisations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best job for a university student?

Private tutoring is often the best overall option for students with strong academic knowledge. It offers flexible scheduling, useful experience and good earning potential. Students without experience may find retail, hospitality or campus work easier to obtain.

What is the best part-time job for students with no experience?

Retail assistant, barista, hospitality worker, campus assistant and delivery rider roles commonly accept beginners.

What are the best online jobs for university students?

Online tutoring, writing, design, social media assistance, virtual administration and data-entry work are common choices. Use verified employers and agree payment terms in writing.

Can international students work while studying?

How many hours should I work during term time?

Many students manage 8 to 12 hours per week, but the right number depends on your course and circumstances. Reduce your hours during examinations where possible.

How can I get a job without a CV?

Contact your university careers service, approach local employers and prepare a short CV focused on skills, availability, coursework and volunteering.

Final Advice

The best student job supports your degree instead of competing with it.

Choose work that fits your timetable, calculate the real income after travel and expenses, and ask clear questions before accepting an offer. Start with fewer hours if you are uncertain. You can increase them later once you understand your academic workload.

If you are planning to study overseas, compare your work options with your course, budget and destination before making a decision. Guidance about studying in the UK, international student support, scholarship options and free study-abroad guidance can help you plan the wider cost of your education.
